metadata.title: Describe When, Not What.
metadata.subtitle: The Agent Development Skill (Prose Triggers)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: when you write a custom Claude Code agent, does listing what it can do get it used at the right time — or does that depend on something else entirely? Lands the carry-out that a subagent only gets called when its description states its trigger conditions, not its capabilities.

beats.narration_text: Someone assumed listing an agent's skills was enough for Claude to know when to use it. It isn't — only its triggers do. So: does listing my agent's triggers tell Claude when to use it?

beats.narration_text: An agent file is two things: YAML frontmatter, then a markdown system-prompt body. Frontmatter has five fields. Name — lowercase with hyphens, three to fifty characters, starting and ending alphanumeric: code-reviewer, test-generator, security-analyzer. Description — the field that matters most, because it's loaded into context whenever the agent is registered, so it's what decides whether Claude dispatches this agent at all. Model — inherit is the recommended default. Color is just visual distinction in the interface. And tools — the array of permissions the agent actually gets; give it only what the task needs. The body underneath spells out the agent's role and output format, plus a When to invoke section with worked scenarios.

The description has one job: state exactly when Claude should reach for this agent — not just what it can do. The format here is: 'Use this agent when...', then 'Typical triggers include' two to four concrete scenarios, then a pointer to a When to invoke section in the body. That prose names real triggers — proactive and reactive, different phrasings of the same request — and says when not to use the agent. The body's own When to invoke section repeats this in more depth: a bold scenario name, what the situation looks like, and what the agent should actually do. Two different jobs: the description is for Claude's dispatch decision; the body is for the agent once it's already running.

Here's the catch with two locations: nothing keeps them in sync. If the trigger scenarios change and only the description gets updated, the body's When to invoke section goes stale — or the other way around. And it's the description alone that Claude reads to decide whether to dispatch the agent at all, so a scenario that only lives in the stale body section never even gets checked at that moment. Keeping both current, by hand, every time triggers change, is the actual maintenance cost of this design.
A subagent only gets called when its description says exactly when to use it — not just what it does. The best agent in the world never fires if its description only lists capabilities.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Create an agent for my plugin that reviews pull request diffs for security issues. Then check the description Claude wrote: does it say 'Use this agent when...' with two to four concrete trigger scenarios, or does it just list what the agent does? Does the body have a When to invoke section with worked scenarios? Are the tools it picked the minimum needed — probably Read and Bash, not Write? That's the actual test of a good agent file.
